lede: Components can be joined in one loop or on separate branches. Each way has a rule for the current and a rule for the voltage, and together the four rules let you fill in any meter reading a question leaves blank.
can: Tell a series circuit from a parallel one by tracing the route the current takes
Use the series rules and the parallel rules to find any missing meter reading
Share a current between two unequal parallel branches

md: Take one cell and two lamps. In one loop, pull a lamp out and the other goes dark; on separate branches, it stays lit. This topic is that difference, and one fact beneath it: charge is never used up going round.

caption: Follow the arrows from the cell back to the cell. One route: series. A route that splits and joins again: parallel.

md: Follow the route from the cell back to the cell. One route through every component in turn is **series**; a route that splits at a **junction** into branches and joins again is **parallel**. Judge by the route, not by how the circuit is laid out on the page.

stem: Circuit X: from the cell the wire passes lamp P, then lamp Q, then returns. Circuit Y: from the cell the wire reaches a junction, lamp P on one path and lamp Q on the other, and the paths meet again before the cell. Which is series and which is parallel? [2]

steps.working: Circuit X: one route, through P and then Q, so X is series.
steps.decision: No junction: the charge has no choice of path.

steps.working: Circuit Y: at the junction the route divides, one lamp on each path, and the paths rejoin, so Y is parallel.
steps.decision: A junction and two paths that meet again: branches.

steps.working: A switch added to either would not change which kind it is.
steps.decision: The near-miss: what sits on a route never changes the route.

prompt: A cell, a switch and two lamps are joined so that the current leaving the cell reaches a junction and can pass through either lamp before the two paths meet again. Which kind of circuit is this?
options: parallel: the route splits at a junction and joins again
series: there is one route round the loop
neither, because the circuit contains a switch
answer: parallel: the route splits at a junction and joins again
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, a route that reaches a junction, divides with one lamp on each path, and meets again is parallel. Series would be one path through both lamps in turn. A switch only opens or closes the route it sits in; it never changes the kind of circuit.

optionNotes.option: series: there is one route round the loop
optionNotes.why: Series has no junction: every charge passes both lamps. Here the route divides, so the charge takes one lamp or the other.

optionNotes.option: neither, because the circuit contains a switch
optionNotes.why: A switch opens or closes a route; it does not decide the kind of circuit. The junction does.

twin.prompt: A cell and two lamps are joined so that the only way round passes the first lamp and then the second. Which kind of circuit is this?
options: series: there is one route round the loop
parallel: the route splits at a junction
neither, because the lamps are different
twin.answer: series: there is one route round the loop
twin.explain: One way round, through each lamp in turn, with no junction: that is series.

optionNotes.option: parallel: the route splits at a junction
optionNotes.why: There is no junction here: the only way round passes both lamps in turn.

optionNotes.option: neither, because the lamps are different
optionNotes.why: What the components are does not matter; the route decides, and here it is one loop.

caption: Three ammeters in one loop, before, between and after the resistors: the same reading at every point.

md: A series circuit is one loop, so the charge passing the first component has nowhere else to go: it passes the second too. **The current is the same at every point.** A component takes energy from the charge, not the charge itself.

title: Why the current is not used up
md: Current is the charge passing a point each second. Charge cannot pile up in a wire or vanish inside a component, so whatever flows into a component flows out of it.

stem: A cell drives a current round a lamp and a buzzer in series. The ammeter before the lamp reads 0.07 A. What do an ammeter between the lamp and the buzzer, and one after the buzzer, read? [2]

steps.working: Between the lamp and the buzzer: 0.07 A.
steps.decision: One loop: the same charge passes every point each second.
Each component takes energy from the charge, never charge from the current.

prompt: In a series circuit an ammeter just before a heater reads 0.24 A. What does an ammeter just after the heater read, in amps?
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, a series circuit is one loop and the heater takes energy, not charge. So the same current flows in and out: the ammeter after the heater reads 0.24 A too.

twin.prompt: A series loop has three lamps. An ammeter next to the first lamp reads 0.45 A. What does an ammeter next to the third lamp read, in amps?
twin.explain: One loop, one current: every ammeter in it reads 0.45 A.

caption: A voltmeter across each resistor: the two readings add up to the supply voltage.

md: Voltage measures the energy each unit of charge carries. The supply gives the charge its energy once, and the components in the loop take that energy in turn. So **in series, the voltages across the components add up to the supply voltage**: the supply is shared out, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

stem: A 5.0 V battery drives a lamp and a motor in series. The voltmeter across the lamp reads 1.8 V. What does a voltmeter across the motor read? [2]

steps.working: In series the voltages across the components add up to the supply.
steps.decision: The supply is shared along the loop.
The missing reading is the supply take away the one you have.

prompt: Two components are in series with a 4.0 V supply. The voltmeter across the first component reads 1.0 V. What does a voltmeter across the second component read, in volts?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, the missing reading is the supply take away the one you have: 4.0 − 1.0 = 3.0 V. Giving the whole 4.0 V would be the parallel rule used on a series circuit.

twin.prompt: Three components are in series with a 9.0 V supply. The voltmeters across the first two read 2.2 V and 3.5 V. What does a voltmeter across the third read, in volts?
twin.explain: The three readings add up to the supply: 9.0 − 2.2 − 3.5 = 3.3 V.

caption: Two different resistors on two branches, and both voltmeters read the supply voltage.

md: Each branch of a parallel circuit is joined straight across the supply, one end to each terminal. So **in parallel, the voltage across every branch is the supply voltage**, whatever is on the branch. That is why every lamp in a house has the full mains voltage across it, however many others are switched on.

stem: A 9.0 V battery feeds three branches in parallel: a lamp, a resistor and a small motor. What voltage is across each branch? [2]

steps.working: Each branch has one end on each terminal of the battery.
steps.decision: Nothing else stands between a branch and the supply.

steps.working: So the lamp, the resistor and the motor each have 9.0 V across them.
steps.decision: Different components, the same voltage: nothing is shared out between branches.

prompt: Three lamps are connected in parallel across a 3 V battery, each lamp on its own branch. What is the voltage across each lamp, in volts?
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, each branch is joined straight across the battery, so each lamp has the whole 3 V across it. Sharing the voltage belongs to series circuits; dividing by 3 would use that rule here.

twin.prompt: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 1.5 V cell, each on its own branch. What is the voltage across each lamp, in volts?
twin.explain: Each branch is joined straight across the cell, so each lamp has the full 1.5 V.

text: 5. Parallel: the currents add at a junction

caption: What flows into a junction flows out of it: the branch currents add up to the main-line current.

md: At a junction the charge divides between the branches, but none of it is lost and none is stored. What flows in equals what flows out. So **in parallel, the current in the main line is the sum of the branch currents**, and where the branches meet again their currents add back together.

stem: A current of 0.65 A arrives at a junction, and the upper branch carries 0.38 A. What does the lower branch carry, and what flows on where the branches join again? [2]

steps.decision: Nothing is lost at a junction, so the branches share what arrived.
The branch currents add back together.

title: Current in parallel circuits
why: A three-minute lesson on the current splitting into branches and joining again. It is made for another board and may draw circuits a little differently; its potential difference is CCEA's voltage.

prompt: A current of 1.5 A flows into a junction and splits between two branches. One branch carries 1.1 A. What current flows in the other branch, in amps?
explain: As in step 1 of the See it, a junction stores nothing, so the two branches share what arrived: 1.5 − 1.1 = 0.4 A.

twin.prompt: Two branch currents of 0.28 A and 0.52 A join again. What current flows on in the main line, in amps?
twin.explain: Where branches join, their currents add: 0.28 + 0.52 = 0.80 A.

md: The paper's favourite shape puts a battery across two equal resistors in parallel, with an ammeter in the main line, one on each branch, and a voltmeter across the battery and across each branch. Fill in every voltage first, then the currents.

stem: In the circuit shown, A3 reads 0.45 A and V3 reads 7.5 V. Find V2, V1, A2 and A1. [4]

steps.decision: V2 is across a branch, so it reads the supply voltage, the same as V3.
V1 is across the battery itself: the supply voltage again.
Equal resistors with equal voltages carry equal currents.
A1 is in the main line, so it carries both branches.

prompt: In the circuit shown, the battery is changed and ammeter A1 in the main line now reads 0.8 A. The two resistors are still equal. What does ammeter A2 on one branch read, in amps?
explain: As in steps 3 and 4 of the See it, A1 feeds both branches, and equal resistors with the same voltage take equal shares. So each branch carries half the main-line current: A2 reads 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4 A.

twin.prompt: In the same circuit a different battery makes A1 read 1.3 A. The resistors are still equal. What does A3 read, in amps?
twin.explain: Equal branches share the main-line current equally: 1.3 ÷ 2 = 0.65 A.

md: Each branch is its own route from one terminal to the other. Take a lamp out of one branch and only that branch breaks: every other branch still has the full supply voltage, so its lamp is just as bright. The main-line current falls, because the charge has one route fewer.

stem: Four identical lamps are in parallel across a battery, and the main-line ammeter reads 1.80 A. One lamp is unscrewed. What happens to the other three lamps, and to the main-line reading? [2]

steps.working: The other three stay exactly as bright.
steps.decision: Each of their branches still has the full battery voltage.

steps.working: Each branch carried $1.80 \div 4 = 0.45$ A, so the main line now carries $3 \times 0.45 = 1.35$ A.
steps.decision: One branch fewer, so one share fewer in the main line.

task: Build a battery with two light bulbs in parallel, one bulb on each branch. Put an ammeter in the main line and read it. Then remove one bulb: watch the other bulb, and the main-line reading.

prompt: Two identical lamps are in parallel across a battery, and the main-line ammeter reads 1.0 A. One lamp is unscrewed. What does the main-line ammeter read now?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, each branch carried an equal share, here 1.0 ÷ 2. With one branch gone, the main line carries only the one share left, half of what it carried. The other lamp stays just as bright.

optionNotes.why: The remaining lamp is unchanged, so it can seem nothing changes; but the main line now carries only its branch.
Nothing doubles: the remaining branch still carries its own share, and the main line loses the other share.

twin.prompt: Three identical lamps are in parallel, and the main-line ammeter reads 1.5 A. One lamp is unscrewed. What does the main-line ammeter read now?
twin.explain: Each branch carried 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 A; two branches are left, so the main line carries 1.0 A.

optionNotes.why: The main line carries the sum of the branches, and one branch has gone.
That is one branch's share; two branches are still working.

md: **Six readings, two given.** Summer 2019 Higher and Summer 2026 Foundation: two equal resistors in parallel. Every voltmeter reads the supply; the branches share the current equally.
**Ammeters either side of the branches** (Summer 2022, both tiers). The main-line ammeter after the branches reads the same as the one before them.
**A resistor feeding an equal pair.** Summer 2021 Foundation gave one branch current in milliamps. The other branch matches it and the single resistor carries both. Convert to amps only for V = I R.

stem: In the figure the two resistors are equal, and A1 reads 2.2 A. Find A2, A3 and A4. [3]

steps.decision: Equal branches share the main-line current equally.
The shares join again, so A4 matches A1.

prompt: In the circuit shown, ammeter A1 reads 0.6 A and the two resistors are equal. What does ammeter A4 read?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, A4 is in the main line after the branches have joined, so it carries the whole current again, the same as A1: 0.6 A. Only the branch ammeters read half of it, and nothing in the circuit doubles a current.

optionNotes.why: That is one branch's share. A4 sits after the branches have joined, where the shares add back together.
The branches do not add to more than arrived: A4 carries exactly what A1 carries.

twin.prompt: In the same circuit a different supply makes A1 read 2.6 A, with the resistors still equal. What does A4 read?
twin.explain: A4 is in the main line after the branches join again, so it reads the same as A1: 2.6 A.

optionNotes.why: That is a branch current. After the join, the branches add back to 2.6 A.
Nothing doubles: what leaves the branches is what entered them.

md: Unequal branches do not split the current in half. Each branch still has the full supply voltage, so its current is that voltage divided by its own resistance, $I = V \div R$ (from V = I R). Twice the resistance takes half the current.

title: Where the Higher paper separates candidates
md: Summer 2023 Higher: most candidates could share a current between equal resistors; only the most able could when one resistance was double the other. Never halve unless the branches are equal.

Twice the resistance, half the current.
The branch currents add.

prompt: A 2.0 V supply drives a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 8 Ω resistor, in amps?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, each branch has the whole supply voltage, so the 8 Ω branch takes 2.0 ÷ 8 = 0.25 A. The 4 Ω branch takes twice as much, 0.50 A.

twin.prompt: A 1.5 V cell drives a 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 3 Ω resistor, in amps?
twin.explain: The 3 Ω branch has the whole 1.5 V: I = 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.50 A.

text: Going further: only the total current given

md: The Higher paper often gives only the current arriving at the branches, not the voltage (Summer 2021 and Summer 2023). The two branches still have the same voltage across them, so the smaller resistance takes the larger share. With one resistance twice the other, the currents are in the ratio 2 : 1: split the total into three equal shares.

stem: A current of 1.50 A arrives at a 55 Ω and a 110 Ω resistor in parallel. Find the current in each. [3]

steps.working: 55 Ω is half of 110 Ω, so the currents are 2 : 1.
steps.decision: Same voltage, half the resistance, twice the current.
Three shares in all.
Check: they add back to the total.

prompt: A current of 1.0 A arrives at a 22 Ω resistor and an 88 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 22 Ω resistor, in amps?
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, both resistors have the same voltage, so the 22 Ω one, a quarter of 88 Ω, takes four times the current. Split 1.0 A into five equal shares: the 22 Ω resistor takes four of them.

twin.prompt: A current of 2.1 A arrives at a 5 Ω resistor and a 10 Ω resistor connected in parallel. What current flows in the 10 Ω resistor, in amps?
twin.explain: The 5 Ω resistor takes twice the 10 Ω one's current: three shares of 0.7 A, one for the 10 Ω resistor.

md:
Trace the route to tell series from parallel.
Series: one current everywhere; the voltages add up to the supply.
Parallel: the supply voltage on every branch; the branch currents add up to the main line.
Fill in a grid of missing ammeter and voltmeter readings, voltages first.
Share a current between unequal branches: twice the resistance, half the current.

These rules arrive as a circuit of ammeters and voltmeters, a mark for each missing reading, and then a V = I R calculation on the same circuit. Trace the route first; fill in every voltage, then the currents. The first mark is the reading that simply repeats; the last usually needs an addition, a subtraction or a milliamp conversion. Stuck? Ask which quantity is the same everywhere and which is shared.
